The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]), let $|T|$ and the singular values $s_n(T)$ be
as in the absolute-value definition
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Let
$J=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$ when $\operatorname{ran}T$ is infinite-dimensional. When
$\operatorname{ran}T$ is finite-dimensional, put
$r:=\dim\operatorname{ran}T\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-dimension]]) and let
$J=\{1,\dots,r\}$, interpreted as $\varnothing$ when $r=0$. Thus $J$ indexes
exactly the positive singular values counted with multiplicity, which we write
as $(s_j)_{j\in J}$ in nonincreasing order. Then:

1. there are orthonormal families $(e_j)_{j\in J}$ in $(\ker T)^\perp$ and
   $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ in $\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$, indexed by exactly $J$,
   with $|T|e_j=s_je_j$ and $f_j=s_j^{-1}Te_j$ for every $j\in J$;
2. for every $x\in H$ the series converges in norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{j\in J}s_j\langle x,e_j\rangle f_j,$$
   and its finite partial sums
   $T_n:=\sum_{j\le n}s_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ satisfy
   $\|T-T_n\|\le s_{n+1}$ for every $n$ with $n+1\in J$ (and $T_n=T$ for
   $n\ge r$ when $r<+\infty$);
3. the linear map $U$ defined on the span of $\{e_j:j\in J\}$ by $Ue_j:=f_j$,
   extended by continuity to $(\ker T)^\perp$ and by zero on $\ker T$, is a
   **partial isometry** with
   $$T=U|T|,\qquad U^*U=P_{(\ker T)^\perp},\qquad U^*U\text{ is the orthogonal projection onto }(\ker T)^\perp,$$
   and $UU^*$ the orthogonal projection onto $\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$;
4. the zero-padded sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ is *not* used to index the
   orthonormal systems: the systems carry exactly the index set $J$ of the
   positive singular values, and the terms $s_n(T)=0$ beyond the rank in the
   finite-rank case are numerical padding only.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact linear operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces (each with a countable dense subset), and assume $T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt, meaning that for its positive singular values $s_j$ the sum $\sum_{j\ge1}s_j^2$ is finite. Put $S=T^*T$, $\lambda_j=s_j^2$, and $\lambda_1=\|S\|$, with the positive eigenvalues listed with multiplicity in nonincreasing order. Let $\varphi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and strictly increasing with $\varphi(0)=0$, and take its inverse on its range. Assume the paper's convexity condition on the spectral range: $x\mapsto x\varphi^{-1}(\sqrt{x})$ is convex for $0\le x\le\varphi(\lambda_1)^2$. Define the source class $\mathcal W_\varphi(\rho):=\{\varphi(S)w:w\in X,\ \|w\|_X\le\rho\}$ for $\rho>0$; equivalently, it is the source ball with singular-value index $\psi(t)=\varphi(t^2)$.

An ordered spectral filter is a family of functions $q_\alpha:[0,\lambda_1]\to[0,\infty)$ indexed by a set $\mathcal A\subset(0,\infty)$ with $0$ as an accumulation point, such that for constants $C_q'<\infty$ and $C_q''=1$,
$$
0\le\alpha q_\alpha(x)\le C_q',\qquad 0\le xq_\alpha(x)\le1,
$$
and $q_\alpha(x)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(x)$ whenever $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, for every $x\in[0,\lambda_1]$. The index function $\varphi$ is a qualification of this filter if for some $C_\varphi<\infty$,
$$
\sup_{0\le x\le\lambda_1}\varphi(x)(1-xq_\alpha(x))\le C_\varphi\varphi(\alpha)\qquad(\alpha\in\mathcal A).
$$

For $\alpha\in\mathcal A$, define the variance function
$$
V_{T,q}(\alpha):=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_\alpha(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
For $\sigma>0$, a decreasing candidate sequence $(\alpha_m)_{m\in\mathbb N_0}$ in $\mathcal A$ has **geometric variance growth** if $V_{T,q}(\alpha_0)>0$ and there are constants $1<\theta_1\le\theta_2<\infty$ such that
$$
\theta_1\le\frac{V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)}{V_{T,q}(\alpha_{m-1})}\le\theta_2\qquad(m\ge1).
$$
Set $v_m:=\sigma^2V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)$ and
$$
u_m:=\sigma^2\sup_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2,
$$
the operator norm of the estimator-noise covariance in the singular basis. The bound $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j<\infty$ make each $u_m$ and $v_m$ finite. The finite candidate set ends at
$$
m_{\max}:=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_0:v_m\ge1\}.
$$
The geometric lower bound $v_m\ge v_0\theta_1^m$ makes this index finite.

Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, where separable means having a countable dense subset, and let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space. A real isonormal Gaussian process on $H$ is a family $Z(g)$ of real random variables with finite second moments, indexed by $g\in H$, such that $g\mapsto[Z(g)]$ is linear into $L^2(\mathbb P)$, $\mathbb E Z(g)=0$, and $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_H$. It is also required that for every finite orthonormal tuple $(e_1,\ldots,e_m)$ the variables $Z(e_1),\ldots,Z(e_m)$ are independent and each has density $\varphi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. For any finite list of vectors, expressing them in an orthonormal basis of their finite-dimensional span shows that their process values have the corresponding linear-image Gaussian law. Here $L^2(\mathbb P)$ identifies square-integrable random variables that agree almost surely. When $H\ne\{0\}$, all unit-vector marginals have the same law; write $N(a,\sigma^2)$ for the law of $a+\sigma Z(e)$ for any unit vector $e\in H$ and $\sigma\ge0$.

Let $X$ be a set, let $\Theta\subseteq X$ be a nonempty parameter set, let $K:X\to H$ be a signal map, and let $\epsilon>0$. For $x\in\Theta$ and $g\in H$, define the observation functional

$$Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g).$$

The associated statistical inverse experiment has sample space $\mathbb R^H$ with the cylinder sigma-algebra generated by the evaluation maps $y\mapsto y(g)$, and its sampling law $P_x$ is the law of the random function $g\mapsto Y_x(g)$. Each sample is indexed by test functionals on $H$; it is not asserted to be a vector in $H$ or to have a continuous path. If $H=\{0\}$, linearity forces $Z(0)=0$ and the experiment is deterministic.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Put $c_j:=\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j$ and $d_j:=\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)$. By [F3], $|c_j|\le|\theta_j|$, so $(c_j)_j\in\ell^2$. Also $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j<\infty$ by [F2], so $\sum_jd_j^2=\sigma^2\sum_j\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2<\infty$. The partial sums of $Q:=\sum_jd_j^2\xi_j^2$ increase, and [F5] gives $\mathbb EQ=\sum_jd_j^2<\infty$. For each integer $r\ge1$, [F6] gives $\mathbb P(Q\ge r)\le\mathbb EQ/r$; since $\{Q=+\infty\}\subseteq\{Q\ge r\}$ for every $r$, $Q<\infty$ almost surely. Thus on a measurable event of probability one the coordinate series $\sum_j(c_j+d_j\xi_j)v_j$ converges in $X$; define its pointwise limit there and set it to zero on the null complement. The finite partial sums are measurable, and their pointwise limit on this event, extended by zero, is measurable because $X$ is separable. By Parseval and [F5], for each $N$, $\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-X_{m,N}\|_X^2=\sum_{j>N}\mathbb E(c_j+d_j\xi_j)^2=\sum_{j>N}c_j^2+\sum_{j>N}d_j^2$, where [F4] gives $\mathbb E\xi_j=0$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$. Both deterministic and noise tails tend to zero, so this constructed measurable pointwise limit is the $L^2(\Omega;X)$ limit. In particular it has finite second moment.

For $m_1<m_2$, [F3] gives $0\le1-\lambda_jq_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)\le1-\lambda_jq_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)$. Squaring these nonnegative terms and summing against $\theta_j^2$ gives $B_{m_2}^2\le B_{m_1}^2$. Moreover, $f_{m_2}-f_{m_1}$ has coordinate $\lambda_j(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}-q_{\alpha_{m_1}})\theta_j$, whose multiplier equals $(1-\lambda_jq_{\alpha_{m_1}})-(1-\lambda_jq_{\alpha_{m_2}})$ and lies between zero and $1-\lambda_jq_{\alpha_{m_1}}$; coordinatewise comparison therefore yields $\|f_{m_2}-f_{m_1}\|_X\le B_{m_1}$.

Subtracting $x$ in each singular coordinate gives deterministic bias coefficient $-(1-\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j))\theta_j$ and centered noise coefficient $\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j$. Since $\mathbb E\xi_j=0$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$ by [F1] and [F4], summing the coordinate second moments and using monotone convergence gives $\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-x\|_X^2=\sum_j(1-\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j))^2\theta_j^2+\sigma^2\sum_j\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2=B_m^2+v_m$.

The centered pairwise noise difference has coordinate variance $\sigma^2\lambda_j(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j))^2$. By [F3], each difference lies between zero and $q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)$; summing its squared value against $\sigma^2\lambda_j$ proves $v_{m_1,m_2}\le v_{m_2}$.

Assume Countable Choice and the positive-noise Gaussian sequence model with $\sigma>0$, a fixed complete positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$ for an injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator $T:X\to Y$, and a truth with coordinates $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$ in $\ell^2$. Write $\lambda_j=s_j^2$ and let $\xi_j$ be the independent standard-normal noise coordinates. Let $q_\alpha$ be nonnegative and satisfy $0\le\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le1$, $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$, and $q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\le q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)$ whenever $m_1<m_2$. For each candidate $m$, form the finite sums
$$
X_{m,N}:=\sum_{j=1}^N\bigl(\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j+\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j\bigr)v_j.
$$
The conclusion below includes the existence of their limit $\widehat x_m$ in $L^2(\Omega;X)$. Put $f_m:=\mathbb E\widehat x_m$, $B_m:=\|f_m-x\|_X$, and $v_m:=\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-f_m\|_X^2$. Then $\widehat x_m$ is a measurable $X$-valued random element with finite second moment and
$$
\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-x\|_X^2=B_m^2+v_m,\qquad v_m=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
If $m_1<m_2$, then $B_{m_2}\le B_{m_1}$, $\|f_{m_2}-f_{m_1}\|_X\le B_{m_1}$, and
$$
v_{m_1,m_2}:=\mathbb E\| (\widehat x_{m_2}-f_{m_2})-(\widehat x_{m_1}-f_{m_1})\|_X^2=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j\bigl(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\bigr)^2\le v_{m_2}.
$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces, let $S=T^*T$, and let $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$ be a fixed positive singular system with $\lambda_j=s_j^2$. Let $Z$ be a real isonormal Gaussian process on $Y$, meaning that $g\mapsto Z(g)$ is linear into $L^2$, is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. In the weak observation experiment $Y_x(g)=\langle Tx,g\rangle_Y+\sigma Z(g)$ with known noise standard deviation $\sigma>0$, use the ordered filter $q_\alpha$, the geometric-variance candidates $\alpha_0>\cdots>\alpha_{m_{\max}}$, and variances $v_m=\sigma^2\sum_j\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2$ from the preceding definition. For each candidate index $m$, the regularized estimator $\widehat x_m$ is the $L^2$ limit of its finite singular-coordinate sums; its $j$th coordinate is $\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j+\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j$, where $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$ and $\xi_j=Z(u_j)$.

Take as input the observed sequence $y=(y_j)_{j\ge1}$, where $y_j:=Y_x(u_j)$. For each candidate $m$ and each $N=1,2,\ldots$, compute
$$
\widehat x_{m,N}^{\mathrm{obs}}:=\sum_{j=1}^N s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)y_jv_j.
$$
If these partial sums converge in $X$, define $\widehat x_m(y)$ to be their limit; otherwise set $\widehat x_m(y)=0_X$. This specifies an $X$-valued output for every input sequence. The quantities $v_{m_1,m_2}$ and $z_{m_1,m_2}(x)$ are determined by the known operator, filter, noise level and Gaussian coordinate law.

For $0\le m_1<m_2\le m_{\max}$, set
$$
v_{m_1,m_2}:=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j\bigl(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\bigr)^2
$$
and let $N_{m_1,m_2}$ be the norm of the centered estimator difference divided by $\sigma$. For $x>0$, define its upper quantile by
$$
z_{m_1,m_2}(x):=\inf\{z\ge0:\mathbb P(N_{m_1,m_2}>z)\le e^{-x}\}.
$$
Given fixed $\beta>0$ and $\gamma>0$, for $0\le m<m_{\max}$ put $x_m:=2(1+\gamma)\log(v_{m+1}/v_0)$, and for each pair $m_1<m_2$ put $\eta_{m_1,m_2}:=\sigma z_{m_1,m_2}(x_{m_1})+\beta\sqrt{v_{m_1,m_2}}$. Accept an index $m_1$ exactly when $\|\widehat x_{m_1}(y)-\widehat x_{m_2}(y)\|_X\le\eta_{m_1,m_2}$ for every $m_2$ with $m_1<m_2\le m_{\max}$, and output the smallest accepted index $\widehat m$ and parameter $\widehat\alpha=\alpha_{\widehat m}$. For $m_1=m_{\max}$, accept without comparisons, including when $m_{\max}=0$. This rule uses only the observed sequence, the known operator and filter, the noise level, the fixed candidate grid, and $\beta,\gamma$; it does not use $x$ or its source index $\varphi$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(\xi_j)_{j\ge1}$ be given real random variables on a probability space such that every finite subfamily is independent and each variable has density $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/2}$. Let $a_j\ge0$ be deterministic with $v:=\sum_j a_j<\infty$, and put $u:=\sup_j a_j$ and $w:=\sum_j a_j^2$. The nonnegative series $Q:=\sum_j a_j\xi_j^2$ is finite almost surely. Define $N:=\sqrt Q$ on that event and set $N=0$ on its null complement. Then
$$\mathbb E N^2=v,\qquad \mathbb E N^4=v^2+2w\le3v^2.$$
For every $t>0$,
$$\mathbb P\{N^2>v+2\sqrt{wt}+2ut\}\le e^{-t},\qquad \mathbb P\{N>\sqrt v+\sqrt{2ut}\}\le e^{-t}.$$
The upper quantile $q(t):=\inf\{z\ge0:\mathbb P(N>z)\le e^{-t}\}$ is finite and satisfies
$$\mathbb P(N>q(t))\le e^{-t},\qquad q(t)\le\sqrt v+\sqrt{2ut}.$$
These conclusions include $v=0$, in which case $N=q(t)=0$ almost surely. For a Gaussian series in a fixed orthonormal coordinate system with coordinate variances $a_j$, $N$ is its norm.

Assume Countable Choice. Put $S=T^*T$, $\lambda_j=s_j^2$, and $\lambda_1=\|S\|$, with the positive eigenvalues listed with multiplicity in nonincreasing order. Let $\varphi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and strictly increasing with $\varphi(0)=0$, and take its inverse on its range. Assume the paper's convexity condition on the spectral range: $x\mapsto x\varphi^{-1}(\sqrt{x})$ is convex for $0\le x\le\varphi(\lambda_1)^2$. Define the source class $\mathcal W_\varphi(\rho):=\{\varphi(S)w:w\in X,\ \|w\|_X\le\rho\}$ for $\rho>0$; equivalently, it is the source ball with singular-value index $\psi(t)=\varphi(t^2)$.

An ordered spectral filter is a family of functions $q_\alpha:[0,\lambda_1]\to[0,\infty)$ indexed by a set $\mathcal A\subset(0,\infty)$ with $0$ as an accumulation point, such that for constants $C_q'<\infty$ and $C_q''=1$,
$$
0\le\alpha q_\alpha(x)\le C_q',\qquad 0\le xq_\alpha(x)\le1,
$$
and $q_\alpha(x)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(x)$ whenever $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, for every $x\in[0,\lambda_1]$. The index function $\varphi$ is a qualification of this filter if for some $C_\varphi<\infty$,
$$
\sup_{0\le x\le\lambda_1}\varphi(x)(1-xq_\alpha(x))\le C_\varphi\varphi(\alpha)\qquad(\alpha\in\mathcal A).
$$

For $\alpha\in\mathcal A$, define the variance function
$$
V_{T,q}(\alpha):=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_\alpha(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
For $\sigma>0$, a decreasing candidate sequence $(\alpha_m)_{m\in\mathbb N_0}$ in $\mathcal A$ has **geometric variance growth** if $V_{T,q}(\alpha_0)>0$ and there are constants $1<\theta_1\le\theta_2<\infty$ such that
$$
\theta_1\le\frac{V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)}{V_{T,q}(\alpha_{m-1})}\le\theta_2\qquad(m\ge1).
$$
Set $v_m:=\sigma^2V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)$ and
$$
u_m:=\sigma^2\sup_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2,
$$
the operator norm of the estimator-noise covariance in the singular basis. The bound $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j<\infty$ make each $u_m$ and $v_m$ finite. The finite candidate set ends at
$$
m_{\max}:=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_0:v_m\ge1\}.
$$
The geometric lower bound $v_m\ge v_0\theta_1^m$ makes this index finite.

[[lem-compact-gram-operator-is-positive-and-has-kernel]], $S$ is compact,

nonzero eigenvalues of $S$ and $P_t$ the orthogonal projection onto the
eigenspace of $t\in\Sigma$; let $P_0$ be the orthogonal projection onto

$q:\{0\}\cup\Sigma\to\mathbb F$ is
$$q(S)x:=q(0)P_0x+\sum_{t\in\Sigma}q(t)P_tx,$$
where the finite-subset net converges in norm by
[[lem-compact-spectral-multiplier-is-well-defined]]. For $\nu>0$, define
$S^\nu$ by the multiplier $q_\nu(0)=0$ and $q_\nu(t)=t^\nu$ for $t>0$.

For $\lambda>0$, the Tikhonov filter and residual filter are
$$g_\lambda(t)=\frac1{t+\lambda},\qquad r_\lambda(t)=1-tg_\lambda(t)=\frac{\lambda}{t+\lambda}.$$
The Tikhonov solution for data $y_\delta\in Y$ is
$$x_\lambda^\delta=g_\lambda(S)A^*y_\delta =(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*y_\delta.$$

$t+\lambda$ on each $E_t$ and $\lambda$ on $\ker S$, so $g_\lambda(S)$ is

constant $C_\nu\ge0$ satisfies

$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

Throughout, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$ is written
$\lambda_n$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]), and
$\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb R$ is the copy of the integers
([[def-integers]]).

**The torus.** Let $q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the
canonical projection of the quotient of the additive group $\mathbb R$ by its
subgroup $\mathbb Z$, carrying the quotient topology
([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-topological-space]]); we write
$[t]:=q(t)=t+\mathbb Z$. Thus $[s]=[t]$ exactly when $s-t\in\mathbb Z$. The map
$q$ is continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and $\mathbb T$ is a compact
Hausdorff space homeomorphic to the Euclidean unit circle.

**Fundamental domain.** Every class has exactly one representative in $[0,1)$:
for $t\in\mathbb R$ the integer part $n=\lfloor t\rfloor$ satisfies
$n\le t<n+1$, so $t-n\in[0,1)$ represents $[t]$ ([[lem-integer-part]]); and if
$s,t\in[0,1)$ satisfy $s-t\in\mathbb Z$, then $|s-t|<1$ forces $s=t$.
Consequently the map $[0,1)\to\mathbb T$, $t\mapsto[t]$, is a bijection.

**Topological checks.** The closed interval $[0,1]$ is compact by [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and maps onto $\mathbb T$, so the quotient is compact by [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. The map $t\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is continuous by [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], and is constant on quotient fibres by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]. It induces a continuous map $\varphi:\mathbb T\to S^1$ by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The bijection of $[0,2\pi)$ with the circle in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]], together with the unique representatives in $[0,1)$, makes $\varphi$ bijective. The Euclidean circle is Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]], so the compact-to-Hausdorff clause of [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]] makes $\varphi$ a homeomorphism. In particular $\mathbb T$ is Hausdorff.

The map $q$ is open: for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, its saturation $q^{-1}[q[U]]=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}(U+k)$ is open. The images under $q$ of rational-endpoint open intervals form a countable base: if $q(t)\in V$ with $V$ open, choose such an interval containing $t$ and contained in $q^{-1}[V]$. Its image is an open neighbourhood contained in $V$.

**The measure.** For a Borel set $E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) the preimage $q^{-1}[E]$ is a Borel subset of
$\mathbb R$, because $q$ is continuous
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]), hence Lebesgue
measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). Define

$$m_{\mathbb T}(E):=\lambda_1\bigl(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)\bigr) ,$$

the value at $q^{-1}[E]$ of the same-ambient restriction of $\lambda_1$ to $[0,1)$
([[def-restriction-of-a-measure]]).

This is a measure on $\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$ by [[prop-restriction-is-a-measure]]:
the assignment $E\mapsto\lambda_1(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1))$ is the composition of the
restriction measure with the inverse image along $q$, and inverse images preserve
the empty set, complements and countable unions, while countable additivity is
that of $\lambda_1$. It is a **probability measure**:
$m_{\mathbb T}(\mathbb T)=\lambda_1([0,1))=1$
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]). Thus
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T})$ is a probability measure space
([[def-measure-space]], [[def-measure]]).

**The integral.** For a Borel measurable $F:\mathbb T\to[0,+\infty]$, define

$$\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}:=\int_{[0,1)}F\circ q\,d\lambda_1 .$$

The defining integral is meaningful because $F\circ q$ is Borel
([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]],
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]). The assignment agrees with
$E\mapsto m_{\mathbb T}(E)$ on indicators, and it is additive and homogeneous on
finite nonnegative simple functions; for a sequence $0\le F_0\le F_1\le\cdots$
with $F_n\uparrow F$ pointwise the identity passes to the limit because
$F_n\circ q\uparrow F\circ q$ and monotone convergence holds for $\lambda_1$
([[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]],
[[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]). For real or complex integrable
$F$ the integral is defined by decomposition into nonnegative parts or into real
and imaginary parts, and it is linear
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]],
[[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]). In particular
$\int_{\mathbb T}1\,dm_{\mathbb T}=1$, and the same formula holds with $[0,1)$
replaced by any half-open interval $[a,a+1)$ or $(a,a+1]$, by the periodicity of
$q^{-1}[E]$ and the translation invariance of $\lambda_1$
([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]).

**Translation invariance.** For $y\in\mathbb R$ the map
$\tau_y:\mathbb T\to\mathbb T$, $\tau_y([t]):=[t+y]$, is well defined (if
$s-t\in\mathbb Z$ then $(s+y)-(t+y)\in\mathbb Z$) and continuous, because it is
induced by the continuous map $t\mapsto q(t+y)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb T$. This composite is constant on the fibres of $q$, since $q(t)=q(s)$ implies $q(t+y)=q(s+y)$ ([[thm-quotient-universal-property]]). It preserves
$m_{\mathbb T}$: write $y=n+r$ with $n=\lfloor y\rfloor$ and $r\in[0,1)$, put
$A:=q^{-1}[E]$ and use that $A-n=A$ and that
$A\cap[0,1)=\bigl(A\cap[0,r)\bigr)\cup\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)$ while
$A\cap[r,r+1)=\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)\cup\bigl((A\cap[0,r))+1\bigr)$, so that

$$m_{\mathbb T}(\tau_y^{-1}E)=\lambda_1\bigl((A-y)\cap[0,1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[r,r+1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[0,1)\bigr)=m_{\mathbb T}(E),$$

the middle equality by translation invariance of $\lambda_1$. Hence
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T},\tau_y)$ is a measure-preserving
system for every $y$, and the published integral-invariance theorem gives
$\int_{\mathbb T}F\circ\tau_y\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}$
for every measurable $F\ge0$ and every integrable $F$
([[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]],
[[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]]). This is the
**normalized Haar integral** of $\mathbb T$; abstract Haar theory is not
invoked.

**The finite torus.** For a natural $n\ge1$ put
$\mathbb T^n:=\mathbb R^n/\mathbb Z^n$ with the quotient topology of the
canonical projection $q_n$, and define

$$m_{\mathbb T^n}(E):=\lambda_n\bigl(q_n^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)^n\bigr),\qquad \int_{\mathbb T^n}F\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}:=\int_{[0,1)^n}F\circ q_n\,d\lambda_n .$$

Coordinatewise integer parts give unique representatives in $[0,1)^n$, and the continuous quotient map sends the compact cube $[0,1]^n$ onto $\mathbb T^n$. Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection
$\Phi:\mathbb T^n\to(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n$ by the universal property. Its
domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite
product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection
theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the
finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]],
[[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]],
[[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters
$x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact
Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets
of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give
$m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so
$m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure
$m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$
([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures,
and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them
on the entire Borel sigma-algebra
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on
$\mathbb T^n$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The characters
$(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z}$ form an orthonormal basis of the complex Hilbert space
$L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]): they are
orthonormal and their closed linear span is all of $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact linear operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces (each with a countable dense subset), and assume $T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt, meaning that for its positive singular values $s_j$ the sum $\sum_{j\ge1}s_j^2$ is finite. Put $S=T^*T$, $\lambda_j=s_j^2$, and $\lambda_1=\|S\|$, with the positive eigenvalues listed with multiplicity in nonincreasing order. Let $\varphi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and strictly increasing with $\varphi(0)=0$, and take its inverse on its range. Assume the paper's convexity condition on the spectral range: $x\mapsto x\varphi^{-1}(\sqrt{x})$ is convex for $0\le x\le\varphi(\lambda_1)^2$. Define the source class $\mathcal W_\varphi(\rho):=\{\varphi(S)w:w\in X,\ \|w\|_X\le\rho\}$ for $\rho>0$; equivalently, it is the source ball with singular-value index $\psi(t)=\varphi(t^2)$.

An ordered spectral filter is a family of functions $q_\alpha:[0,\lambda_1]\to[0,\infty)$ indexed by a set $\mathcal A\subset(0,\infty)$ with $0$ as an accumulation point, such that for constants $C_q'<\infty$ and $C_q''=1$,
$$
0\le\alpha q_\alpha(x)\le C_q',\qquad 0\le xq_\alpha(x)\le1,
$$
and $q_\alpha(x)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(x)$ whenever $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, for every $x\in[0,\lambda_1]$. The index function $\varphi$ is a qualification of this filter if for some $C_\varphi<\infty$,
$$
\sup_{0\le x\le\lambda_1}\varphi(x)(1-xq_\alpha(x))\le C_\varphi\varphi(\alpha)\qquad(\alpha\in\mathcal A).
$$

For $\alpha\in\mathcal A$, define the variance function
$$
V_{T,q}(\alpha):=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_\alpha(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
For $\sigma>0$, a decreasing candidate sequence $(\alpha_m)_{m\in\mathbb N_0}$ in $\mathcal A$ has **geometric variance growth** if $V_{T,q}(\alpha_0)>0$ and there are constants $1<\theta_1\le\theta_2<\infty$ such that
$$
\theta_1\le\frac{V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)}{V_{T,q}(\alpha_{m-1})}\le\theta_2\qquad(m\ge1).
$$
Set $v_m:=\sigma^2V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)$ and
$$
u_m:=\sigma^2\sup_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2,
$$
the operator norm of the estimator-noise covariance in the singular basis. The bound $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j<\infty$ make each $u_m$ and $v_m$ finite. The finite candidate set ends at
$$
m_{\max}:=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_0:v_m\ge1\}.
$$
The geometric lower bound $v_m\ge v_0\theta_1^m$ makes this index finite.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces, let $S=T^*T$, and let $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$ be a fixed positive singular system with $\lambda_j=s_j^2$. Let $Z$ be a real isonormal Gaussian process on $Y$, meaning that $g\mapsto Z(g)$ is linear into $L^2$, is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. In the weak observation experiment $Y_x(g)=\langle Tx,g\rangle_Y+\sigma Z(g)$ with known noise standard deviation $\sigma>0$, use the ordered filter $q_\alpha$, the geometric-variance candidates $\alpha_0>\cdots>\alpha_{m_{\max}}$, and variances $v_m=\sigma^2\sum_j\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2$ from the preceding definition. For each candidate index $m$, the regularized estimator $\widehat x_m$ is the $L^2$ limit of its finite singular-coordinate sums; its $j$th coordinate is $\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j+\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j$, where $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$ and $\xi_j=Z(u_j)$.

Take as input the observed sequence $y=(y_j)_{j\ge1}$, where $y_j:=Y_x(u_j)$. For each candidate $m$ and each $N=1,2,\ldots$, compute
$$
\widehat x_{m,N}^{\mathrm{obs}}:=\sum_{j=1}^N s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)y_jv_j.
$$
If these partial sums converge in $X$, define $\widehat x_m(y)$ to be their limit; otherwise set $\widehat x_m(y)=0_X$. This specifies an $X$-valued output for every input sequence. The quantities $v_{m_1,m_2}$ and $z_{m_1,m_2}(x)$ are determined by the known operator, filter, noise level and Gaussian coordinate law.

For $0\le m_1<m_2\le m_{\max}$, set
$$
v_{m_1,m_2}:=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j\bigl(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\bigr)^2
$$
and let $N_{m_1,m_2}$ be the norm of the centered estimator difference divided by $\sigma$. For $x>0$, define its upper quantile by
$$
z_{m_1,m_2}(x):=\inf\{z\ge0:\mathbb P(N_{m_1,m_2}>z)\le e^{-x}\}.
$$
Given fixed $\beta>0$ and $\gamma>0$, for $0\le m<m_{\max}$ put $x_m:=2(1+\gamma)\log(v_{m+1}/v_0)$, and for each pair $m_1<m_2$ put $\eta_{m_1,m_2}:=\sigma z_{m_1,m_2}(x_{m_1})+\beta\sqrt{v_{m_1,m_2}}$. Accept an index $m_1$ exactly when $\|\widehat x_{m_1}(y)-\widehat x_{m_2}(y)\|_X\le\eta_{m_1,m_2}$ for every $m_2$ with $m_1<m_2\le m_{\max}$, and output the smallest accepted index $\widehat m$ and parameter $\widehat\alpha=\alpha_{\widehat m}$. For $m_1=m_{\max}$, accept without comparisons, including when $m_{\max}=0$. This rule uses only the observed sequence, the known operator and filter, the noise level, the fixed candidate grid, and $\beta,\gamma$; it does not use $x$ or its source index $\varphi$.

Assume Countable Choice and the positive-noise Gaussian sequence model with $\sigma>0$, a fixed complete positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$ for an injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator $T:X\to Y$, and a truth with coordinates $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$ in $\ell^2$. Write $\lambda_j=s_j^2$ and let $\xi_j$ be the independent standard-normal noise coordinates. Let $q_\alpha$ be nonnegative and satisfy $0\le\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le1$, $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$, and $q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\le q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)$ whenever $m_1<m_2$. For each candidate $m$, form the finite sums
$$
X_{m,N}:=\sum_{j=1}^N\bigl(\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j+\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j\bigr)v_j.
$$
The conclusion below includes the existence of their limit $\widehat x_m$ in $L^2(\Omega;X)$. Put $f_m:=\mathbb E\widehat x_m$, $B_m:=\|f_m-x\|_X$, and $v_m:=\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-f_m\|_X^2$. Then $\widehat x_m$ is a measurable $X$-valued random element with finite second moment and
$$
\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-x\|_X^2=B_m^2+v_m,\qquad v_m=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
If $m_1<m_2$, then $B_{m_2}\le B_{m_1}$, $\|f_{m_2}-f_{m_1}\|_X\le B_{m_1}$, and
$$
v_{m_1,m_2}:=\mathbb E\| (\widehat x_{m_2}-f_{m_2})-(\widehat x_{m_1}-f_{m_1})\|_X^2=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j\bigl(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\bigr)^2\le v_{m_2}.
$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Fix a measurable integrable representative, also denoted by $f$, if $L^1([a,b])$ is interpreted as a space of almost-everywhere equivalence classes. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then there is a measurable set $E\subseteq(a,b)$ whose complement in $(a,b)$ has Lebesgue measure zero such that $F$ is differentiable at every $x\in E$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\in E).$$
The primitive $F$ is independent of the chosen representative; the almost-everywhere derivative identity holds for every fixed measurable integrable representative.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue regular-distribution convention. If $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is nonempty, open and connected and $\partial_j u=0$ for every $1\le j\le n$, then there is a unique $c\in\mathbb C$ such that $u(\psi)=c\int\psi$ for every test. Conversely every constant regular distribution has zero first derivatives. On a disconnected open set constants may differ on different connected components.

derivations.claim: The functions $e_j(x)=\sqrt2\sin(\pi jx)$ are orthonormal on $(0,1)$ by the product-to-sum identities and direct integration. If $h\in L^2(0,1)$ is orthogonal to all of them, its odd extension to $(-1,1)$, continued periodically with period $2$, has zero constant and cosine coefficients by oddness and zero sine coefficients by the assumed orthogonality. Rescaling to the circle in [F1], every Fourier coefficient of this extension vanishes; completeness in [F2] therefore makes the extension, and hence $h$, zero almost everywhere. Thus $(e_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis, and [F7] supplies the real Hilbert structure used below.

For $f\in L^2(0,1)$, [F8] gives $f\in L^1(0,1)$. Since $0\le G(x,t)\le1/4$, $|Tf(x)|\le\|f\|_1/4\le\|f\|_2/4$ for every $x$, so the integral formula defines a bounded linear operator from $L^2(0,1)$ to itself. The kernel formula also gives
$$(Tf)(x)=(1-x)\int_0^x t f(t)\,dt+x\int_x^1(1-t)f(t)\,dt.$$
The two indefinite integrals are absolutely continuous by [F9], and [F10] gives their derivatives almost everywhere. They show that $Tf$ is continuous, has zero endpoint values, and has first derivative almost everywhere equal to the absolutely continuous function $g(x)=-\int_0^x tf(t)\,dt+\int_x^1(1-t)f(t)\,dt$, whose derivative is $g'(x)=-xf(x)-(1-x)f(x)=-f(x)$ almost everywhere. To verify the claimed distributional equation directly, take any $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,1)$. The function $(x,t)\mapsto G(x,t)f(t)\phi''(x)$ is integrable on $(0,1)^2$, so [F11] permits reversing the integrals; splitting at $x=t$ and integrating the smooth test function twice gives
$$\int_0^1(Tf)(x)\phi''(x)\,dx =\int_0^1 f(t)\left(\int_0^1G(x,t)\phi''(x)\,dx\right)dt =-\int_0^1 f(t)\phi(t)\,dt.$$
Thus $(Tf)''=-f$ in distributions. If two continuous Dirichlet solutions exist, their difference $h$ has $h''=0$ in distributions. Applying [F12] to $h'$ makes $h'$ constant, and applying it to $h-cx$ makes $h$ affine; continuity identifies the distribution with its pointwise affine representative. The two zero endpoint values force $h=0$.

For every $\lambda\ge0$, the Tikhonov filter is nonnegative and satisfies $\alpha q_\alpha(\lambda)=\alpha/(\lambda+\alpha)\le1$ and $\lambda q_\alpha(\lambda)=\lambda/(\lambda+\alpha)\le1$. If $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, then $\lambda+\widetilde\alpha<\lambda+\alpha$, so $q_\alpha(\lambda)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(\lambda)$. Thus the Tikhonov family is an ordered filter with $C_q'=1$.

Since $-e_j''=(\pi j)^2e_j$ and $e_j(0)=e_j(1)=0$, uniqueness of the Dirichlet solution from step 1.2 gives $Te_j=(\pi j)^{-2}e_j$. Completeness from step 1.1 therefore diagonalizes $T$ and $T^*T$, with singular values $s_j=(\pi j)^{-2}$ and eigenvalues $\lambda_j=(\pi j)^{-4}$. All singular values are positive, so $T$ is injective. The truncations $T_Nf=\sum_{j=1}^N(\pi j)^{-2}\langle f,e_j\rangle e_j$ have finite rank and satisfy $\|T-T_N\|=\sup_{j>N}(\pi j)^{-2}\to0$, so $T$ is compact. Also $\sum_j s_j^2=\pi^{-4}\sum_jj^{-4}<\infty$ by comparison with $\int_1^\infty x^{-4}\,dx$, so $T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt.

For the Tikhonov filter, put $V(\alpha):=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j(\lambda_j+\alpha)^{-2}$. On every compact interval $[a,b]\subset(0,\infty)$ its summands are continuous and bounded above by $\lambda_j/a^2$, a summable sequence by step 1.3, so $V$ is continuous there. Each summand strictly decreases with $\alpha$. Also $V(\alpha)\le\alpha^{-2}\sum_j\lambda_j\to0$ as $\alpha\to\infty$. For every fixed $j$, $V(\alpha)\ge\lambda_j(\lambda_j+\alpha)^{-2}\to1/\lambda_j$ as $\alpha\downarrow0$; since $\lambda_j\to0$, these lower bounds show $V(\alpha)\to\infty$. Given $c>0$ and $\theta>1$, continuity and strict decrease give a unique $\alpha_m>0$ with $V(\alpha_m)=c\theta^m$ for each $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Thus $\alpha_m$ decreases to zero and $v_m=\sigma^2V(\alpha_m)$ has consecutive ratio $\theta$, so [F4] holds.

Direct integration of the two pieces of $f^\dagger$ gives $\langle f^\dagger,e_j\rangle=2\sqrt2\sin(\pi j/2)/(\pi^2j^2)$. On the first half, $g^\dagger(x)=-x^3/6+x/8$, so $g^{\dagger\prime\prime}(x)=-x$; on the second half, $g^\dagger(x)=x^3/6-x^2/2+3x/8-1/24$, so $g^{\dagger\prime\prime}(x)=x-1$. The two values at $x=1/2$ both equal $1/24$, and both first derivatives there equal zero; the endpoint values are zero. Hence $-g^{\dagger\prime\prime}=f^\dagger$ weakly with Dirichlet boundary values, so uniqueness from step 1.2 gives $Tf^\dagger=g^\dagger$. The sequence model in [F3] and the filter conditions in [F4] therefore supply an admissible white-noise input to the finite selector in [F5], whose estimates are well-defined by [F6].

For every $n\ge1$, $t_n>0$ and $t_n\to0$ exponentially since $R>1$. The ratio of consecutive squared multipliers is $((n+1)/n)^2((n+2)/(n+1))^2R^{-2}$, which tends to $R^{-2}<1$; choose $\rho$ strictly between $R^{-2}$ and $1$, then the ratio is at most $\rho$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Thus $\sum_{n\ge1}2t_n^2<\infty$. The operator is injective because all its diagonal multipliers are positive. Its truncation to frequencies $n\le N$ is finite rank and the operator-norm error is $\sup_{n>N}t_n\to0$, so $T_R$ is compact and Hilbert–Schmidt.

The frequency multipliers satisfy $t_{n+1}/t_n=(n+2)/(nR)$, which can exceed $1$ for small $n$; thus the frequency order is not always the singular-value order. The multiset of modes has a nonincreasing enumeration: at every stage a remaining maximum exists because $t_n\to0$ and only finitely many modes lie above any fixed positive threshold, and the fixed tie rule selects one uniquely. Every mode is eventually listed because only finitely many modes have multiplier at least its positive multiplier. The operator is diagonal on the orthonormal cosine–sine basis, so the frequency eigenvalue is $\mu_n=t_n^2=n^2(n+1)^2R^{-2n-4}$ twice at each frequency, and the enumerated singular system has these values in nonincreasing order. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces, let $S=T^*T$, and let $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$ be a fixed positive singular system with $\lambda_j=s_j^2$. Let $Z$ be a real isonormal Gaussian process on $Y$, meaning that $g\mapsto Z(g)$ is linear into $L^2$, is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. In the weak observation experiment $Y_x(g)=\langle Tx,g\rangle_Y+\sigma Z(g)$ with known noise standard deviation $\sigma>0$, use the ordered filter $q_\alpha$, the geometric-variance candidates $\alpha_0>\cdots>\alpha_{m_{\max}}$, and variances $v_m=\sigma^2\sum_j\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2$ from the preceding definition. For each candidate index $m$, the regularized estimator $\widehat x_m$ is the $L^2$ limit of its finite singular-coordinate sums; its $j$th coordinate is $\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j+\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j$, where $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$ and $\xi_j=Z(u_j)$.

Take as input the observed sequence $y=(y_j)_{j\ge1}$, where $y_j:=Y_x(u_j)$. For each candidate $m$ and each $N=1,2,\ldots$, compute
$$
\widehat x_{m,N}^{\mathrm{obs}}:=\sum_{j=1}^N s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)y_jv_j.
$$
If these partial sums converge in $X$, define $\widehat x_m(y)$ to be their limit; otherwise set $\widehat x_m(y)=0_X$. This specifies an $X$-valued output for every input sequence. The quantities $v_{m_1,m_2}$ and $z_{m_1,m_2}(x)$ are determined by the known operator, filter, noise level and Gaussian coordinate law.

For $0\le m_1<m_2\le m_{\max}$, set
$$
v_{m_1,m_2}:=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j\bigl(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\bigr)^2
$$
and let $N_{m_1,m_2}$ be the norm of the centered estimator difference divided by $\sigma$. For $x>0$, define its upper quantile by
$$
z_{m_1,m_2}(x):=\inf\{z\ge0:\mathbb P(N_{m_1,m_2}>z)\le e^{-x}\}.
$$
Given fixed $\beta>0$ and $\gamma>0$, for $0\le m<m_{\max}$ put $x_m:=2(1+\gamma)\log(v_{m+1}/v_0)$, and for each pair $m_1<m_2$ put $\eta_{m_1,m_2}:=\sigma z_{m_1,m_2}(x_{m_1})+\beta\sqrt{v_{m_1,m_2}}$. Accept an index $m_1$ exactly when $\|\widehat x_{m_1}(y)-\widehat x_{m_2}(y)\|_X\le\eta_{m_1,m_2}$ for every $m_2$ with $m_1<m_2\le m_{\max}$, and output the smallest accepted index $\widehat m$ and parameter $\widehat\alpha=\alpha_{\widehat m}$. For $m_1=m_{\max}$, accept without comparisons, including when $m_{\max}=0$. This rule uses only the observed sequence, the known operator and filter, the noise level, the fixed candidate grid, and $\beta,\gamma$; it does not use $x$ or its source index $\varphi$.

Assume Countable Choice and the positive-noise Gaussian sequence model with $\sigma>0$, a fixed complete positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$ for an injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator $T:X\to Y$, and a truth with coordinates $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$ in $\ell^2$. Write $\lambda_j=s_j^2$ and let $\xi_j$ be the independent standard-normal noise coordinates. Let $q_\alpha$ be nonnegative and satisfy $0\le\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le1$, $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$, and $q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\le q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)$ whenever $m_1<m_2$. For each candidate $m$, form the finite sums
$$
X_{m,N}:=\sum_{j=1}^N\bigl(\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j+\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j\bigr)v_j.
$$
The conclusion below includes the existence of their limit $\widehat x_m$ in $L^2(\Omega;X)$. Put $f_m:=\mathbb E\widehat x_m$, $B_m:=\|f_m-x\|_X$, and $v_m:=\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-f_m\|_X^2$. Then $\widehat x_m$ is a measurable $X$-valued random element with finite second moment and
$$
\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-x\|_X^2=B_m^2+v_m,\qquad v_m=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
If $m_1<m_2$, then $B_{m_2}\le B_{m_1}$, $\|f_{m_2}-f_{m_1}\|_X\le B_{m_1}$, and
$$
v_{m_1,m_2}:=\mathbb E\| (\widehat x_{m_2}-f_{m_2})-(\widehat x_{m_1}-f_{m_1})\|_X^2=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j\bigl(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\bigr)^2\le v_{m_2}.
$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact linear operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces (each with a countable dense subset), and assume $T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt, meaning that for its positive singular values $s_j$ the sum $\sum_{j\ge1}s_j^2$ is finite. Put $S=T^*T$, $\lambda_j=s_j^2$, and $\lambda_1=\|S\|$, with the positive eigenvalues listed with multiplicity in nonincreasing order. Let $\varphi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and strictly increasing with $\varphi(0)=0$, and take its inverse on its range. Assume the paper's convexity condition on the spectral range: $x\mapsto x\varphi^{-1}(\sqrt{x})$ is convex for $0\le x\le\varphi(\lambda_1)^2$. Define the source class $\mathcal W_\varphi(\rho):=\{\varphi(S)w:w\in X,\ \|w\|_X\le\rho\}$ for $\rho>0$; equivalently, it is the source ball with singular-value index $\psi(t)=\varphi(t^2)$.

An ordered spectral filter is a family of functions $q_\alpha:[0,\lambda_1]\to[0,\infty)$ indexed by a set $\mathcal A\subset(0,\infty)$ with $0$ as an accumulation point, such that for constants $C_q'<\infty$ and $C_q''=1$,
$$
0\le\alpha q_\alpha(x)\le C_q',\qquad 0\le xq_\alpha(x)\le1,
$$
and $q_\alpha(x)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(x)$ whenever $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, for every $x\in[0,\lambda_1]$. The index function $\varphi$ is a qualification of this filter if for some $C_\varphi<\infty$,
$$
\sup_{0\le x\le\lambda_1}\varphi(x)(1-xq_\alpha(x))\le C_\varphi\varphi(\alpha)\qquad(\alpha\in\mathcal A).
$$

For $\alpha\in\mathcal A$, define the variance function
$$
V_{T,q}(\alpha):=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_\alpha(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
For $\sigma>0$, a decreasing candidate sequence $(\alpha_m)_{m\in\mathbb N_0}$ in $\mathcal A$ has **geometric variance growth** if $V_{T,q}(\alpha_0)>0$ and there are constants $1<\theta_1\le\theta_2<\infty$ such that
$$
\theta_1\le\frac{V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)}{V_{T,q}(\alpha_{m-1})}\le\theta_2\qquad(m\ge1).
$$
Set $v_m:=\sigma^2V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)$ and
$$
u_m:=\sigma^2\sup_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2,
$$
the operator norm of the estimator-noise covariance in the singular basis. The bound $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j<\infty$ make each $u_m$ and $v_m$ finite. The finite candidate set ends at
$$
m_{\max}:=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_0:v_m\ge1\}.
$$
The geometric lower bound $v_m\ge v_0\theta_1^m$ makes this index finite.

The real sequence space
$$\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)=\left\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|x_n|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with its canonical inner product and norm from
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]], is complete and
therefore is a real Hilbert space.

derivations.claim: Interleaving the constant coordinate and cosine–sine pairs is a linear isometry onto real $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, so [F7] gives the stated real Hilbert structure. The real Fourier modes are orthonormal by taking real and imaginary parts of the character basis in [F1]. On each positive frequency, $\partial_{xx}\cos(nx)=-n^2\cos(nx)$ and $\partial_{xx}\sin(nx)=-n^2\sin(nx)$, so solving $\partial_tu=\partial_{xx}u$ multiplies both coefficients by $e^{-n^2\bar t}$; the constant mode is unchanged. Therefore the operator in the Example is the periodic heat forward map in Fourier coordinates.

Every multiplier of $T_{\bar t}$ is positive, so $T_{\bar t}$ is injective. The positive-frequency multipliers tend to zero, so finite-frequency truncations converge in operator norm and $T_{\bar t}$ is compact. Moreover, $\sum_{n\ge1}2e^{-2n^2\bar t}<\infty$ by comparison with the geometric series $\sum_{n\ge1}2e^{-2n\bar t}$, so the operator is Hilbert–Schmidt. Squaring the multipliers gives the stated eigenvalues of $T_{\bar t}^*T_{\bar t}$.

For spectral cut-off, the inverse-eigenvalue contribution at frequency $n$ is $2e^{2n^2\bar t}$. Since $V_{n-1}\le(2n-1)e^{2(n-1)^2\bar t}$,
$$
\frac{V_n}{V_{n-1}}=1+\frac{2e^{2n^2\bar t}}{V_{n-1}}\ge1+\frac{2}{2n-1}e^{2(2n-1)\bar t}\longrightarrow\infty.
$$
Hence no finite $\theta_2$ bounds all consecutive ratios in this sequence, as claimed.

For every $\lambda\ge0$, $q_\alpha(\lambda)=(\lambda+\alpha)^{-1}$ is nonnegative, $\alpha q_\alpha(\lambda)\le1$, and $\lambda q_\alpha(\lambda)\le1$. If $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, then $\lambda+\widetilde\alpha<\lambda+\alpha$, so $q_\alpha(\lambda)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(\lambda)$. Thus it is an ordered filter with $C_q'=1$ by [F6]. Its variance is $V(\alpha)=1/(1+\alpha)^2+2\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-2n^2\bar t}(e^{-2n^2\bar t}+\alpha)^{-2}$. On each compact interval $\alpha\ge a>0$, the summands are continuous and bounded by $2a^{-2}e^{-2n^2\bar t}$, a summable sequence, so $V$ is continuous there by uniform convergence. It is strictly decreasing. For $\alpha\ge1$, $V(\alpha)\le\alpha^{-2}(1+2\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-2n^2\bar t})\to0$ as $\alpha\to\infty$. It tends to infinity as $\alpha\downarrow0$: for every $N$, its first $N$ positive-frequency terms tend to $2\sum_{n=1}^N e^{2n^2\bar t}$, and these partial sums are unbounded in $N$. The intermediate value theorem therefore selects recursively a decreasing sequence with any prescribed fixed ratio $\theta_1>1$ between consecutive variance values; its upper ratio is the same $\theta_1$. The estimator and each finite comparison are well-defined by [F3]–[F5].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim: Put $Q_n=\sum_{j\le n}a_j\xi_j^2$, $v_n=\sum_{j\le n}a_j$, and $w_n=\sum_{j\le n}a_j^2$. On finite intervals integration by parts with $\phi'(x)=-x\phi(x)$ gives $\int x^{2k}\phi(x)\,dx=[-x^{2k-1}\phi(x)]+(2k-1)\int x^{2k-2}\phi(x)\,dx$. The boundary terms vanish at infinity; the integrals converge since a polynomial times $e^{-x^2/2}$ is bounded by a constant times $e^{-x^2/4}$, whose integral is finite by [F3] and the given unit Gaussian integral. Starting from $\int\phi=1$ therefore gives $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^4=3$. Thus $\mathbb E Q_n=v_n$ and finite independence gives $\mathbb E Q_n^2=v_n^2+2w_n$. Also $u\le v$ and $w\le uv\le v^2$.

The measurable series $Q_n\uparrow Q$ satisfies $\mathbb E Q=v$ by [F1]; hence $Q<\infty$ almost surely, since [F2] gives $\mathbb P(Q\ge r)\le v/r$ for every $r>0$. Extending $N$ by zero on the null exceptional set does not change an integral. Applying [F1] also to $Q_n^2\uparrow Q^2$ proves $\mathbb E N^4=v^2+2w\le3v^2$.

Suppose $u>0$. For $0<s<(2u)^{-1}$ the scalar substitution $y=\sqrt{1-2sa_j}\,x$ in [F3], using the supplied unit density, gives $\mathbb E e^{s a_j\xi_j^2}=(1-2sa_j)^{-1/2}$. Finite factorization [F4] and the power-series inequality $-\log(1-z)-z\le z^2/[2(1-z)]$ for $0\le z<1$ therefore give $$\log\mathbb E e^{s(Q_n-v_n)}=\sum_{j\le n}\left[-sa_j-\tfrac12\log(1-2sa_j)\right]\le\frac{s^2w_n}{1-2us}.$$ If $w_n>0$, apply [F2] to this exponential and choose $s=\sqrt t/(\sqrt{w_n}+2u\sqrt t)$. Substitution gives $-s(2\sqrt{w_nt}+2ut)+s^2w_n/(1-2us)=-t$, so $\mathbb P\{Q_n>v_n+2\sqrt{w_nt}+2ut\}\le e^{-t}$. If $w_n=0$, then $Q_n=v_n=0$ almost surely and this inequality is immediate.

The deterministic levels $v_n+2\sqrt{w_nt}+2ut$ converge to $v+2\sqrt{wt}+2ut$. Whenever $Q$ strictly exceeds this final level, sufficiently large $n$ have $Q_n$ exceeding their corresponding levels. The probability of this eventual-event set is at most the lower limit of their probabilities, as follows directly by countable additivity applied to unions of intersections. Step 2.2 thus gives the first tail inequality. Since $w\le uv$ and $v+2\sqrt{uvt}+2ut\le(\sqrt v+\sqrt{2ut})^2$, the second follows. If $u=0$, all weights vanish and both bounds hold directly.

The second tail bound makes the set defining $q(t)$ nonempty and implies $0\le q(t)\le\sqrt v+\sqrt{2ut}$. This set is upward closed. Every $q(t)+1/n$ therefore belongs to it: by the definition of an infimum some member lies strictly below that number. The events $\{N>q(t)+1/n\}$ increase to $\{N>q(t)\}$, so countable additivity gives $\mathbb P(N>q(t))\le e^{-t}$. When $v=0$, step 2.1 gives $N=0$ almost surely and the quantile is zero. Finally, in a fixed orthonormal system the squared norm of the finite Gaussian sum is $Q_n$; finiteness of $Q$ gives norm convergence of that series and the asserted norm interpretation.
